newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Loyola sees '96 direct investment rising.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Loyola sees '96 direct investment rising.

text.p: Brazilian Central Bank chief Gustavo Loyola said direct foreign investment should increase to between $8 billion and $9 billion this year and continue rising in 1997 as the government's privatization program gains momentum.
Loyola, speaking to reporters after a lunch with Sao Paulo's financial executives, also said the country's economy would grow at a rate of 6.0 to 7.0 percent in the fourth quarter.
Foreign direct investment in Brazil totalled $3.0 billion in 1995, and $1.0 billion in 1994. From January to September this year, foreign direct investment amounted to $5.8 billion.
According to Loyola, increased direct investment will help the country finance its growing trade deficit, which analysts predict will reach between $900 million and $1.0 billion in October.
"What is important is the capacity to finance that deficit," said Loyola, adding that forty percent of the gap can be easily financed through direct investment.
He attributed the deficit to the restructuring and modernization now underway in the Brazilian economy.

"The country is more likely to show deficits than surpluses, and this is normal," he said. "For next year, everyone expects direct investment to rise due to privatizations, especially of the telecommunications and energy sectors."
He said, "Foreign investment is here, taking its risks, everything is normal."
Loyola also attributed recent "market nervousness" to investors taking a short-term day-to-day perspective rather than looking at the longer term, which he said is positive.
"The market is always seeking volatility in order to make money", he said.
